articles.title: Manipulated old clip of Indonesia volcano falsely shared as recent
articles.summary: Indonesia's Mount Semeru saw a surge in volcanic activity in September 2026, but footage circulating online supposedly depicting a recent blast is a manipula...
articles.body:
Indonesia's Mount Semeru saw a surge in volcanic activity in September 2026, but footage circulating online supposedly depicting a recent blast is a manipulated version of a nearly year-old clip. The original video shows a major eruption of Java island's highest peak in November 2025; an analysis found errors suggesting AI tools were used to make the visual more dramatic.

"The status of Mount Semeru's activity today, Saturday, September 12, 2026," reads part of an Indonesian-language TikTok post shared the same day.

"Breaking News. Mount Semeru erupted 29 times in 6 hours. People were prohibited from doing activities within a 5 km radius," reads the video's overlaid text.

The video shows a roadside recording of a volcano emitting fiery explosions and spewing a thick wall of ash into the air.

A person speaking in Javanese can be heard saying, "Don't panic, don't panic, don't be confused."

The video was also shared on X and Facebook with similar claims after Mount Semeru spewed ash 1,000 metres (3,280 feet) above its peak on September 6 ( archived link ).

Authorities raised the alert status to level III, the second-highest level, and people were advised against any activities within a 13-kilometre (eight-mile) radius, the state-run Antara news agency reported.

As of September 16, Semeru remained at level III, according to the Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry ( archived link ).

Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire , where tectonic plates collide, causing frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions ( archived link ).

Mount Anak Krakatau erupted in early September, forcing the main airport serving the capital Jakarta to close ( archived link ).

In late August, increasing volcanic activity at Mount Sinabung in North Sumatra province led to the evacuation of hundreds of people ( archived link ).

However, the circulating video does not show a recent eruption.

A reverse image search on Google led to a similar clip shared on TikTok on November 19, 2025 by an account that frequently shares videos about the volcano (archived here and here ).

"Semeru had a major eruption today," the caption reads.

A man can be heard speaking in Indonesian: "Semeru eruption on November 19, 2025, at 16.00 past 9 minutes. Stay alert."

An AFP video taken during the November 2025 eruption shows a similar white plume rising into the sky ( archived link ). At least 300 people were evacuated at the time, according to Indonesia's National Disaster Agency.

The clip shared in the false posts also matches Google Maps street imagery of a small shop on a street near Mount Semeru ( archived link ).

Moreover, an analysis of the circulating video found several visual elements had been added or changed.

These include the fiery explosions not found in the original clip, as well as the presence of additional scooters fleeing the volcano and a Toyota logo that has been changed to an unknown brand.

The Hive Moderation detection tool found that the video was 94.2% likely to have been generated using AI ( archived link ).

AFP has debunked more misinformation related to Indonesia's volcanoes .

articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two earthquakes struck Nepal's northwestern Mugu district within three hours early Wednesday. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage..
articles.body: Two earthquakes struck Nepal's northwestern Mugu district within three hours early Wednesday. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.According to Nepal's National Earthquake Monitoring and Research Center, the first earthquake, measuring 4.5, struck at 1.51am, followed by a 4.2-magnitude tremor at 4.28am. Both had their epicentre around Kalai in Mugu district.National Center for Seismology (NCS) independently recorded both earthquakes, though it put the magnitude of the second at 4.0. The agency recorded the first quake at 1.36am IST at a depth of 81 km, around 159 km east of Pithoragarh in Uttarakhand.The second was recorded at 4.13am IST at a depth of 98km, about 166km east of Pithoragarh.The latest tremors came days after a 5.3-magnitude earthquake struck Mustang district on September 8, followed by another measuring 4.0 in the same district on September 9.The earthquakes come as Nepal continues to recover from the devastating August 26 Bhote Koshi flash floods, which swept through the Rasuwa-Trishuli river system and several downstream districts. At least 1,403 bodies have been recovered, while 4,089 people remain on the official missing list, according to the latest Nepal Police update. articles.title: She started raising butterflies at 7; by 16, this Florida girl had tracked birds and found populations rose by up to 159% after habitat restoration, she's now headed to a national magazine
articles.summary: US News: A 16-year-old student from Sarasota, Florida, Sophia Haakman began growing butterflies at just 7. Over the years, her love for nature and its beings h.
articles.body: A 16-year-old student from Sarasota, Florida, Sophia Haakman began growing butterflies at just 7. Over the years, her love for nature and its beings has evolved into a serious conservation effort. Haakman sought to find out if the hundreds of hours she spent rehabilitating local ecosystems were truly beneficial to wildlife. So she created her own bird monitoring initiative and a national birding magazine is set to publish the findings.From watching birds to studying their habitatsHaakman's passion for conservation and nature started at a young age. She remembers raising butterflies at the age of 7 and reading a field guide that shifted her interest to birds a few years later. Noticing her affinity for nature, her parents often took her outside.Her mother, Irene, said her daughter found an attachment to Celery Fields, not just because of its diverse environment, but because there were volunteers she could learn from. As an educator, Irene said she has enjoyed watching her daughter turn that curiosity into action, building relationships throughout the local conservation community and being involved in many of the organisations she still works with today. “In the same way as everybody else who has helped her in the community, our job has been to say yes,” Irene Haakman told Suncoast Searchlight. “Sometimes it’s all you can do.”Haakman, a student at Pine View School, has gathered more than 850 volunteer hours across organisations including Sarasota Bay Watch, Sarasota Audubon Society, Suncoast Science Center/Faulhaber Fab Lab and the Florida Young Birders Club. While working with Sarasota Bay Watch, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving local ecosystems, she spent hundreds of hours helping remove invasive plants, restore native habitats and inspire other young people to connect with the environment.The teenager told Suncoast Searchlight that she feels a deep sense of attachment to Sarasota's unique bird populations. “You can’t help but notice them,” Sophia said. “It’s like how when you get a new car, you start seeing it everywhere. Once you learn something about the environment, it’s very hard to forget when you start noticing it around.”As she grew older, Haakman looked for ways to turn her fascination with local wildlife and birds into action. She proposed measuring what happened to birds after restoration. After consulting researchers and experts, she and other volunteers began conducting monthly bird counts from kayaks. Her project found that local bird species were doing better in restored areas than in locations that had not undergone the same habitat work.Ronda Ryan, executive director of Sarasota Bay Watch, said the teenager's work helped the organisation go beyond simply removing invasive species by providing evidence that restoration was supplying birds with resources they needed.Research headed to a national magazineSophia wrote an article about her bird monitoring project and it will be featured in the fall issue of Birding, the American Birding Association's flagship magazine focused on bird identification and conservation. For the teenager, joining Bay Watch, which typically relies on about 25 to 35 volunteers, was her first big step into community engagement upon entering high school.“Being in Sarasota Bay Watch has really allowed me to open up as a person,” she said. “I would not be where I am right now without people in the community helping me and supporting me.”Her journey has not been simple and quick. While her connection to the environment came naturally, she was a socially reserved person and began her work with local organisations as a shy, yet committed volunteer. She used to be terrified of class presentations, but last year, she spoke at a Sarasota County Commission meeting alongside Sarasota Audubon members against a proposed housing project near the Celery Fields bird sanctuary. Though the developer, D.R. Horton, is still pushing for approval, the plan has been repeatedly rejected by commissioners. “Now, I can go to the county commission and talk for two minutes,” she said. “I’m still nervous, but I can do it, and that’s a whole different story. I can speak in front of hundreds of people, and that’s something that I wasn’t able to do before.”Apart from this, at 13, she also helped create the Manasota chapter of the Florida Young Birders Club, giving young birders in Sarasota and Manatee area a place to connect without making the long trip to Tampa. “She just persisted because it wasn’t just for her to do it, but she wanted other kids to be able to do it as well,” Irene Haakman said. “She doesn’t keep it to herself; it’s like there’s this outward sharing of the things that she loves. That’s really what I’ve just been amazed at, how much of a community connector she is.”As a rising senior, Haakman is now exploring colleges. Being a dual US and Canadian citizen, she is open to institutions in either country. Wherever she lands, she said, she plans to major in environmental studies and eventually find work in biophilic design, which would allow her to help make cities more eco-friendly.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: AI-generated image misrepresented as leaders' selfie at BRICS Summit
articles.summary: World leaders travelled to India for the BRICS annual summit in September 2026, but a picture circulating online that appears to show them gathering for a se...
articles.body:
World leaders travelled to India for the BRICS annual summit in September 2026, but a picture circulating online that appears to show them gathering for a selfie during the conference is AI-generated. The image shows a former Iranian president who died years ago and others who were not present at the event, while OpenAI's detection tool has flagged it was made with the tech giant's AI model.

"A single photo has taken the entire world by storm!" reads a Bengali-language Facebook post shared on September 13, 2026.

The attached image appears to show Russian President Vladimir Putin taking a selfie with the heads of state of other BRICS member nations.

It was shared elsewhere on Facebook , Instagram and X following the 18th BRICS Summit hosted in the Indian capital New Delhi on September 12 and 13, where leaders from the bloc discussed ways to foster "inclusive global growth" ( archived link ).

They also issued a joint statement calling for "maximum restraint" in the Middle East war as it "does not serve the common interests of the international community" ( archived link ).

BRICS was created in 2009 by Brazil, China, Russia and India as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers ( archived link ).

It was soon joined by South Africa and was further expanded to include countries such as Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), which hold widely divergent positions on the war in the Middle East.

But the circulating image was not taken during the BRICS Summit in New Delhi.

The picture shows certain leaders -- such as Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva , Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan -- who were not present at the summit, according to the list of participants published by the Indian Ministry of External Affairs ( archived link ).

Brazil's Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan attended the summit instead, while no delegation from Turkey was present.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian was at the summit, but the picture instead shows Ebrahim Raisi , a former president who died in a helicopter crash in 2024 ( archived link ).

Furthermore, the BRICS logo and the phrase used in the image differ from those used at the 2026 New Delhi summit, as seen in handout photos distributed by AFP.

OpenAI's image verification tool detected an invisible SynthID watermark in the image, indicating the image was generated using the company's AI tools (archived here and here ).

AFP has previously fact-checked a similar claim about BRICS in Arabic .

articles.title: ‘Getting punched in the face’: Photos reveal aftermath of Iran strikes on US bases
articles.summary: Middle East News: New photos exclusively obtained by CBS News are helping ascertain the devastating level of damage caused to multiple US bases across the Middle East f.
articles.body: New photos exclusively obtained by CBS News are helping ascertain the devastating level of damage caused to multiple US bases across the Middle East following Iranian missile and drone attacks.The photos were provided to CBS News by active-duty US service members who spoke on condition of anonymity, citing strict military restrictions on media access.“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told CBS News. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”A photo taken at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia, shows a direct hit on the rear section of a Boeing E-3 Sentry aircraft. Its tail was severed from the charred fuselage, which housed a rotating radar system used for collecting airborne intelligence.Photos from the base also showed buildings and barracks gutted by the attacks. Some damaged structures stood beside intact concrete “T-walls” that had been used as fortifications against threats such as grenades and mortars.CBS News also obtained photos showing significant damage at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a major staging area for US Army ground troops, armoured vehicles and some aircraft in a remote desert region northwest of Kuwait City.The images showed destroyed trailers, damaged buildings and a vehicle that appeared to have been hit in the Iranian attacks.Another photo showed the aftermath at Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, with a building bearing visible damage.The new images come as the Defense Department’s inspector general this week released a report on the war in Iran that disclosed up to $3.7 billion in “equipment losses”, including nearly 60 aircraft. According to the report, US Central Command had recorded Iranian strikes on American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.The service member who spoke to CBS News also disputed the characterisation that Iranian attacks were merely isolated weapons slipping through US defences.“These are not ‘squirters’ getting through,” the service member said, referring to language used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after a March 1 attack on Kuwait’s Port of Shuaiba that killed six US troops.“We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed,” the service member told CBS News.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
